title: Spotting Pseudoscience
objective: After this level you can spot pseudoscience by its untestable claims and its habit of moving the goalposts.
summary: Pseudoscience is non-science posing as science. Two questions expose it: could its claims fail, and what do its promoters do when a test goes against them?

cards.headline: A bracelet that "rebalances your energy field." Lab-inspired. Quantum-tuned.
cards.body: It sounds as if a lab made it. But sounding scientific and being scientific are different things. Two questions tell them apart, and neither needs a lab.

cards.headline: Science in costume
cards.body: Many writers describe pseudoscience as non-science posing as science: it isn't scientific, but its promoters try to make it look that way. It can borrow the whole costume, with conferences, journals and associations that share science's surface features but not its quality standards. Remember Level 6's misleading "so"? The word alone proves nothing; the job it does is what counts.

cards.headline: Question one: could it fail?
cards.body: One philosopher's list of warning signs includes an unwillingness to test, ignoring results that go against the theory, and tests arranged so the theory can only be confirmed, never disconfirmed. An "energy field" that no instrument could ever detect fails Level 62's test before it starts: there's no observation that could count against it.

cards.headline: Question two: what happens after a miss?
cards.body: Many pseudoscientific claims have in fact been tested, and failed. What gives them away is the reply. Instead of accepting the result, promoters move the goalposts: they change the requirements after the attempt, so success always stays out of reach. "It only works if you believe in it." That's Level 65's ad hoc rescue, used again and again.

mascot.line: Be kind to people and tough on claims. Ask: could it fail? And what happens when it does?

cards.headline: Pseudoscience: spotted
learned: Pseudoscience is non-science posing as science
Ask whether a claim could ever fail
Watch what happens after a failed test
Moving the goalposts is an ad hoc rescue on repeat

questions.prompt: Match each idea about pseudoscience with its partner.
questions.explanation: Pseudoscience is non-science posing as science. The first question to ask is "Could it fail?", and the second is "What happens after a miss?"

questions.prompt: A remedy fails a fair test, and its seller says the test room "blocked the energy". How is the seller treating the result?

options.label: Accepting that the remedy failed
options.rationale: The seller refuses to accept it.

options.label: Moving the goalposts to dodge the failure
Making a risky new prediction
options.rationale: Nothing new could be checked here.

options.label: Asking for the test to be replicated fairly
options.rationale: The excuse rules out the test instead of asking for another.

questions.explanation: Changing the requirements after a failed attempt, so success stays out of reach, is moving the goalposts.

questions.prompt: A word like "so" doesn't prove an argument is there. What's the matching lesson for lab-sounding words?

options.label: Lab words show a product was tested
options.rationale: Pseudoscience borrows the words without the testing.

options.label: Long words are a sign a claim is false
options.rationale: Words alone prove nothing either way.

options.label: A journal name makes any claim properly scientific
Scientific words don't make a claim scientific

questions.explanation: Just as "so" can appear without an argument, science words can appear without science. Check the job, not the vocabulary.
